v1.1.0 — protocol 2: downtime costs stake; and a node on a home line that dials only a few peers

**Install this before protocol 2 activates.** This release runs the chain exactly as before until
stakers vote protocol 2 in and its activation height is reached. A node on an older release stops
cleanly at that height — it keeps its data and its RPC, and goes on as soon as this release is
installed — but while it is stopped it signs nothing, and if more than a third of the validators'
voting power is stopped, the chain stops with it. Replace the binary and restart; no reset, data,
key and stake stay.

**Protocol 2 — what changes once it is active**

The rest of the set does the work of a validator that is down: every time it is that validator's
turn to propose, the chain waits 12 seconds before the next one takes over. On 2026-10-14 three
validators were silent for over an hour, and the chain ran at a third of its pace. Jailing was the
only consequence, and it taught nothing. From protocol 2:

- **A downtime jail is slashed and the HLX burned:** 1 % of the validator's stake and of its
  delegators' pool for the first jail within about 30 days, 3 % for the second, 5 % for every one
  after that. The wait before `helix tx unjail` grows the same way: 300 blocks, about a day, about
  a week. `GET /validators` shows `recent_downtime_jails`. Burned rather than paid to the rest of
  the set: a proposer chooses whose signatures its certificate carries, and paying the set for
  another validator's misses would pay it to leave them out.
- **A validator that has just become active starts with a downtime debt of 2,400** (of the 3,600
  that jail): one whose node does not sign is jailed after 600 blocks instead of 1,800. Signing pays
  it off within hours. Until now a validator could be promoted on its heartbeat alone and then never
  sign a block — one was, on 2026-10-14.
- **A validator left jailed is unbonded:** a week after it could have unjailed, its own stake moves
  to the unbonding queue (7 days, still slashable) and is its owner's again after that. Its stake
  stops counting toward the two thirds every governance vote needs.

How it is voted in: any validator proposes it — `helix governance propose-upgrade 2 --at-height
<height>` — and it passes with yes-votes from two thirds of all staked HLX:

```bash
helix governance list                            # find its id
helix governance vote <id> --key validator-key.json
```

The activation height is part of the proposal; it lies after the 1000-block vote and at most about
30 days ahead. Keep a margin above the 10,000 HLX minimum: a validator staked at exactly the minimum
falls below it with its first downtime slash. Details:
[Slashing and jailing](https://github.com/silvra-net/helix/blob/master/docs/staking.md#slashing-and-jailing).

**A node on a home connection**

- `HELIX_P2P_OUTBOUND_PEERS=<n>` (at least 3): this node dials at most that many peers itself.
  Every peer passes every message on to every other, so a node hears each vote once per peer; the
  production validator on a home line received 2.2 MB/s from twelve peers it had dialed and 0.9–1.0
  MB/s from four, signing as many blocks. Peers that dial in are still accepted.
- The validator guide: [Running a validator](https://github.com/silvra-net/helix/blob/master/docs/validator-guide.md)
  — from an empty machine to a signing validator, with settings for a data center, a home line and
  a small machine.

**Desktop wallet**

- A wallet that still had the old public address (`helix.silvra.net`, gone since August) in its
  node field failed every request with "error sending request". It now forgets that address and
  reads from `node.silvra.net`.
- **Settings → Use a different wallet…** sets the current wallet aside — the file is renamed and
  kept, never deleted — and opens the start screen to restore another from its 24 words or create
  one. Until now the only way was to find `wallet.json` in the app's data folder by hand.

**Smaller things**

- A node serving its RPC with `HELIX_RPC_SYNC_RATE` set answers the block list (`/blocks/range`) and
  a joiner's checkpoint and snapshot (`/sync/checkpoint`, `/sync/snapshot`) without waiting behind
  the paced block batches it is sending to other joiners — they waited up to 30 s and then answered
  503.
- `helix account` describes `missed_blocks` as what it is, a downtime debt, not "consecutive blocks
  … reset on the next one".
- A state snapshot carries what protocol 2 adds after the state, so snapshots of 1.0.x and of this
  release are readable by both.
